title: Market Pulse: Softer PPI Fails to Reverse the Technology Selloff
summary: October producer inflation undershot the monthly consensus, but broadening input costs, elevated Treasury yields and renewed semiconductor selling kept risk appetite under pressure. Verification pending: independent human editorial review of all linked claims remains outstanding.
reviewed_by: BLAQUE BAUX automated research; human factual verification pending

sections.heading: What changed: observed
paragraphs: October final-demand PPI rose 0.3% month over month versus a 0.4% consensus, after September's revised 1.4% increase. Annual producer inflation accelerated to 6.5%. Goods prices increased 0.5%, services 0.2%, and goods excluding food and energy 0.5%. Electronic components and accessories prices rose 4.2% in October, according to Reuters' review of the release.

Compared with the morning's tentative futures stabilization, Friday's cash-session technology selling intensified: Reuters reported the Nasdaq down more than 1%, the Philadelphia semiconductor index down about 4%, and Nvidia down about 3% in its intraday report. These are reported snapshots, not closing returns.

Reuters reported the two-year Treasury yield near 4.855%, after touching 4.892% earlier, and the dollar at a 19-month high. WTI was reported near $88.44 and Brent near $95.70, both modestly lower on the day. Synchronized cash VIX, investment-grade and high-yield spreads, and issuer CDS were not independently established.

sections.heading: What mattered: interpretation
paragraphs: The softer headline monthly PPI did not resolve the inflation problem: core goods and freight-related cost pressures suggest that disinflation is uneven. AI infrastructure is exposed on both sides of the ledger, through higher component procurement prices and the cost of financing long-duration assets.

The equity response indicates that investors are still reassessing semiconductor concentration and Nvidia leadership execution risk. It does not independently prove an industrywide decline in demand or a broad deterioration in borrower credit quality. Higher Treasury yields and dollar strength are more directly observable constraints on risk assets.

sections.heading: What we are watching
list: Late-session and closing breadth: whether semiconductor losses spread beyond technology, and whether volatility confirms the move.
Next week's retail-sales and Federal Reserve communications; changes in December policy pricing and the two-year Treasury yield.
AI supply-chain price pass-through, contracted capacity, customer free cash flow and actual issuer borrowing spreads.
Oil shipping conditions and the distinction between falling spot crude and persistent transportation or input-cost inflation.

sections.heading: Where we see things going
paragraphs: If subsequent inflation readings ease and corporate credit remains orderly, selective stabilization is plausible. If producer-cost breadth persists alongside higher financing rates, leveraged infrastructure operators may remain more vulnerable than cash-generative suppliers. Neither case supports a precise probability or index target on current evidence.

signal: BLAQUE BAUX Signal: A below-consensus headline PPI print did not translate into a technology recovery. Rising electronic-component costs and elevated financing rates matter simultaneously; follow the cash-flow and credit transmission through AI suppliers, operators and lenders.
